title: LINQ: how do you identify a query that is unexpectedly expensive?
description: Learn to spot LINQ performance traps such as deferred execution, accidental Cartesian products, and repeated enumeration in .NET code.

data.text: LINQ is one of C#'s most expressive features, but its convenience can hide expensive work. Interviewers ask this because a single poorly written query can turn a fast API endpoint into a bottleneck.

The key insight is that LINQ is not a single thing. `IEnumerable<T>` queries execute in memory with delegates. `IQueryable<T>` queries build expression trees that a provider — often Entity Framework Core — translates to SQL. The performance characteristics and failure modes are completely different.
Deferred execution means the query does not run when you write it; it runs when you enumerate it. This is efficient for composition, but dangerous if you accidentally enumerate inside a loop.

data.title: N+1 query pattern
data.text: If a repository method returns `IQueryable<T>` and the caller loops over it while accessing navigation properties, Entity Framework may issue one query per row. Always inspect the generated SQL.
Joining two collections in memory with `SelectMany` or multiple `from` clauses produces every combination. If both collections are large, the result set can grow exponentially.

data.title: Hidden Cartesian explosion
data.content: This query looks innocent but can produce thousands of rows if either collection is large.

data.text: Never guess whether a query is expensive. Use logging, EF Core's `ToQueryString()`, or a profiler. In production, track the query duration and row count in application telemetry.

data.title: Investigation steps
items: Enable EF Core sensitive data logging in development and inspect `ToQueryString()` output.
Add execution-time logging around repository methods.
Compare `IQueryable<T>` versus `IEnumerable<T>` boundaries to see where evaluation happens.
Profile memory allocations if the query materializes large intermediate collections.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Deferred execution is powerful but can cause repeated execution inside loops.
Always inspect the SQL generated by `IQueryable<T>` providers.
Watch for Cartesian products when joining in-memory collections.
Measure with logs and profilers before refactoring.
data.takeaway: A LINQ query is only as efficient as the execution plan it creates — and where you enumerate it.
